fiveRoom.name: Five-room dungeon

placement.title: The five-room dungeon
placement.why: A simple method to write a short, complete adventure, ideal for one session. It chains five key moments: a guardian at the entrance, a challenge that can't be solved with a sword, a setback, the climax, then the reward. The "dungeon" can be any place: a manor, a ship, a forest, a masked ball… Start by choosing where to file the adventure in your campaign.
placement.example: A crypt under a village chapel, where a relic was stolen. Or a smuggler's ship, on the night it sets sail.

frame.title: The setting
frame.why: Before the rooms, lay down the essentials: a name, a place, and above all a hook. The hook is why the characters go there now. If it concerns them personally, they will commit on their own.
frame.example: "The stolen reliquary": the village priest, a friend of one PC, vanished with the relic. He was seen going down into the crypt, and the pilgrimage arrives in three days.

stakes.title: What the players want, and what they risk
stakes.why: The players must know what they came to do, or they will wander. And failure must cost something: that's what creates tension.
stakes.example: Goal: bring the relic back before the pilgrimage. Stakes: without it, the village loses its protection, and the priest will be blamed for the theft.

room1.title: Room 1: the entrance and its guardian
room1.why: Something stops anyone from getting in. It starts the adventure right away, and explains why nobody has conquered this place yet. The guardian doesn't have to be a monster: a guard to convince or a dangerous passage work too.
room1.example: An old spectral guardian blocks the crypt stairs. He lets through anyone who proves they came to protect the relic, not steal it.

room2.title: Room 2: the challenge
room2.why: Here, a sword isn't enough: a puzzle, a negotiation, a place to explore carefully. It lets non-fighters shine, and changes the pace after the entrance.
room2.example: A hall of identical tombs: only the founder's opens, and the clues are in the epitaphs.

room3.title: Room 3: the setback
room3.why: A trap, a red herring or a nasty surprise: things get complicated right before the climax. The characters' resources run low, tension rises.
room3.example: The priest is found… but he is the thief. He was bewitched, and he just triggered the collapse of the gallery.

room4.title: Room 4: the climax
room4.why: The big confrontation, the most intense moment of the adventure. To make it memorable, give the opponent a goal other than fighting, and terrain that changes the game.
room4.example: The enchantress wants to finish the ritual before dawn. She fights while protecting the circle of candles: putting it out weakens her, but reaching it means crossing icy water.

room5.title: Room 5: the reward or the revelation
room5.why: The ending rewards the effort: a treasure, an ally, knowledge. It's also the right time for a twist that opens what comes next in your campaign.
room5.example: The relic is saved, and the freed priest becomes an ally. But the circle bore a symbol: that of a brotherhood the PCs have already met elsewhere.

fiveRoom.tagline: A short adventure in five beats in a single place: a guardian, a challenge, a setback, the climax, the reward.

guided.chooserIntro: Pick a structure: the wizard asks you the right questions, step by step, then creates the chapter and its scenes. You can write everything yourself, or start from an idea and let the AI suggest answers that you then edit.
guided.reviewClock: A "{{name}}" clock with {{segments}} segments will be created in each playthrough of the campaign.

investigation.name: Node-based investigation
investigation.tagline: An investigation that never gets stuck: three leads that cross-reference each other, a conclusion reached by three paths, and a fallback scene if the table stalls.
investigation.reviewLinks: The scenes will be linked by {{count}} leads and clues: each lead points to the others and to the conclusion.

placement.title: Where to put the investigation?
placement.why: The investigation becomes a chapter. Put it in an existing arc or create a new one.
placement.example: An arc "The season of ashes" grouping several cases.

mystery.title: The mystery
mystery.why: Start with the truth: what really happened, who is responsible and why. The players will only learn it at the end, but everything else follows from it: each clue is a trace left by that truth.
mystery.example: The notary poisoned his partner to hide a debt and framed the stable boy. If no one stops him, he'll leave town with the inheritance in three days.

hook.title: The hook
hook.why: The opening scene starts the case and gives the players several leads to follow, not just one. The more it concerns them directly, the more involved they'll be.
hook.example: The stable boy, a friend of one character, is arrested in front of them. He shouts his innocence and mentions the notary, a burnt letter and a maid who saw everything.

node1.title: First lead
node1.why: A lead is a place, a person or an event where the players learn something. Note what they find there: the wizard will link each lead to the two others and to the conclusion.
node1.example: The notary's office: a forged ledger, ashes of a letter in the hearth, and a scribbled address.

node2.title: Second lead
node2.why: Vary the sources: if every lead is an interrogation, a table that doesn't like talking will miss everything. A place, a person, an event: each has its own style.
node2.example: The terrified maid who saw the notary leave the room that night. She'll only talk in exchange for protection.

node3.title: Third lead
node3.why: This lead points back to the two others: players can start with any of them and still find their way. Think about what could go wrong here.
node3.example: The partner's funeral: the notary gives a speech that's too perfect, and the doctor whispers that the body smelled of almonds.

conclusion.title: The conclusion
conclusion.why: All three leads lead here: if the players miss one, they still arrive. Plan how the truth comes out and what the players can do with it.
conclusion.example: Faced with the evidence, the notary tries to flee by the docks. The players can arrest him, hand him to the crowd or bargain for the stable boy's release.

proactive.title: The fallback
proactive.why: If the investigation stalls, this scene comes to the players: the enemy strikes back, a witness comes forward, things get worse. It brings new leads to the three others.
proactive.example: One night, someone tries to set fire to the stable where the stable boy sleeps. The arsonist drops a button from the notary's coat.

review.title: Summary
review.why: Check the scenes before creating the chapter. Everything can be edited afterwards, and the editor review will point out what's missing.

villainPlan.name: The villain's plan
villainPlan.tagline: An enemy who acts even when the players do nothing: six steps, three hidden then three visible, and a clock to track their progress.

placement.title: Where to put the plan?
placement.why: The plan becomes a chapter whose scenes are events to trigger across sessions. Put it in an existing arc or create a new one.
placement.example: The campaign's main arc, so the threat weighs on everything else.

villain.title: The enemy
villain.why: A good enemy wants something the characters own, protect or love: that's what makes the conflict unavoidable. Also say what happens if they succeed.
villain.example: Lady Ysolde, the regent, wants the throne of the young prince the characters swore to protect. If she succeeds, the prince vanishes and the city falls under martial law.

step1.title: Step 1 — Prepare in secret
step1.why: The first three steps are hidden: the enemy moves their pieces without showing themselves. Each still leaves a trace that attentive players can notice.
step1.example: Ysolde replaces the guard captain with one of her men. A guard friendly to the characters is transferred without explanation.

step2.title: Step 2 — Gain allies
step2.why: Each step brings the enemy closer to their goal and hits a little harder than the last. Think about what directly affects a character.
step2.example: She buys the chamberlain's silence. A character's mentor, who refuses, is accused of theft.

step3.title: Step 3 — Set the trap
step3.why: Last hidden step: everything is in place. If the players followed the traces, this is when they can still stop it all.
step3.example: She brings in mercenaries disguised as merchants. An inn the characters frequent fills with armed strangers.

step4.title: Step 4 — Strike
step4.why: From here on, the plan becomes visible: the enemy acts openly. Always leave the players a chance to react, even late.
step4.example: The prince falls ill at the banquet. Ysolde announces she will rule alone "for the good of the realm".

step5.title: Step 5 — Crush the resistance
step5.why: The enemy goes after those who could stop them, often the characters themselves or their loved ones.
step5.example: The guard raids the characters' allies. A wanted poster bears one of their faces.

step6.title: Step 6 — Reach the goal
step6.why: If nothing stopped them, the enemy gets what they wanted. The final confrontation often happens here, but it may also come too late.
step6.example: Ysolde's coronation at the temple. The characters have until the end of the ceremony to save the prince.

clock.title: The plan's clock
clock.why: A six-segment clock, one per step, fills across sessions when the players don't intervene. It's created in each playthrough of the campaign, so you can see how far the enemy has got.
clock.example: Between two sessions, if nobody hindered them, the enemy moves one step forward: fill one segment.

review.title: Summary
review.why: Check the steps before creating the chapter. The scenes aren't linked to each other: it's the enemy who moves forward, and you trigger each step at the right time.
